title: What an action means depends on where you are

unit.title: What an action means depends on where you are
unit.needIt: The same act can be polite in one place and an insult in another. Rules change behavior partly by changing what an act says about you.
unit.why: The professor explains how social norms act like invisible rules for behavior. He shares how wearing a seatbelt or having a compost heap can mean different things depending on where you live.
unit.outcome: Identify how social norms shape the meaning of your everyday actions.
unit.reachesYou: You see this when you decide how to dress for a job interview or a party. You feel it when you follow unwritten rules at a grocery store or a park.
unit.do: Observe one social norm today and think about what message it sends to others. Ask yourself if that message is what you actually want to convey.

quiz.q: How does Sunstein define social norms?
quiz.why: Sunstein defines them as social attitudes of approval and disapproval.
quiz.quote: Social norms are basically social attitudes of approval and disapproval that specify, through the kinds of tacit mechanisms that human beings as social primates have, for for expressing disapproval and approval of one's and others' action.

choices: Demanding more to give up an owned object
quiz.why: It is the tendency to value owned objects more than unowned ones.
quiz.quote: Sunstein, in that article, you may recall, introduces a a discussion of what's known as the endowment effect, which is basically the tendency of human beings to demand more to give up an owned object than they would be prepared to pay to acquire that object.

quiz.q: What is System 1 in dual processing?
quiz.why: System 1 is described as automatic, effortless, and fast.
quiz.quote: System 1 is unconscious or pre-conscious, where a system 2 is conscious. System 1 is automatic, where a system 2 is controlled. System 1 is effortless, where a system 2 is effortful. System 1 is fast, where a system 2 is slow.

quiz.q: What is Hobbes' aim for the social contract?
quiz.why: Hobbes believes we enter a contract for our own practical benefit.
quiz.quote: Hobbes argues that it is of prudential utility for us to engage in a social contract.

quiz.quote: Nozick, in contrast to Rawls, is concerned with how things actually came into being.
